### Factor Manipulation with Tidyverse:

All stringr functions begin with str\_ and take a string vector as their first argument. They wrap regular expressions in a consistent, readable interface.

```{r}
# loading the tidyverse libary
library(tidyverse)
```

### **Detection:**

Detects a pattern in a string and returns a logical values of true or false.The functions for string detection include: str_detect, str_starts, str_ends, etc

```{r}
top_unis <- c("Stanford University", "UC Berkeley", "MIT", "Caltech")
#[1] detect 
str_detect(top_unis, "University")
```

```{r}
# you can use the boolean mask provided to filter the top_unis vector
top_unis[str_detect(top_unis,"University")]
```

```{r}
#[2] str_start(): finds 
names <- c('Matilda','Jemimah','Martha','Gracilda','Samantha')
str_starts(names,'Ma')
# let's filter out those names 
names[str_starts(names,'Ma')]
```

```{r}
# str_end : detects end pattern of string
str_ends(names,'da')
names[str_ends(names,'da')]
```

```{r}
#[3] str_count : counts the number of occurence of a pattern
oral <- 'The world is a small place for us to fight'
str_count(oral,'s')
```

```{r}
# let's try it with our vector: if it is a vector it loops through each vector and counts the pattern it finds:
str_count(names,'a')
```

### Extraction:

Pull out parts of a string

#### **a. str_sub()**

```{r}
#[1] str_sub(string,start,end) : makes a substring from position start to end 
dates <- c("2024-01-15", "2023-12-10")
str_sub(dates, 1, 4)  # we extract characters from position 1 to 4
```

**Note: In str_sub() when you reassign a sub string to any value, it recreates a copy of the original variable with the same name but not modify in place.**

```{r}
# masking senstive data: 
phones <- c("0241234567", "0559876543")

# the substrings are replaced with  four stars to hide those numbers:
str_sub(phones, 4, 7) <- "****"
phones
```

```{r}
#[2] str_extract(string, pattern) : extract first occurence of a string pattern
# finds the first match of a digit in the string: there is none
str_extract(names,"\\d")
```

#### b. str_extract()

Extract the first occurrence of a specified pattern in a string: very powerful in cleaning messy text or extracting information

```{r}
# Example 1: let's extract the id in this patient information
text <- "PatientID: GH-2345 | Test: HIV | Result: Positive"
str_extract(text,"GH-\\d+")

```

```{r}
# Example 2 : let's extract this phone number
text <- "Call me on 024-123-4567 tomorrow"
str_extract(text, "\\d{3}-\\d{3}-\\d{4}")
```

```{r}
# Example 3: Let's try to extract an email address
text <- "Contact: john.doe@gmail.com for follow-up,samuelabugare@gmail.com"
str_extract(text, "[a-zA-Z0-9._%+-]+@[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+")

# see that it matches only the first occurence of the pattern
```

You'd see that str_extract() only extracts the first match; what if we want all the matches

#### str_extract_all()

Extract all matches of the regular pattern from the string

```{r}
# Example 1 : Let's use the same contact text 
str_extract_all(text, "[a-zA-Z0-9_.%-+]+@[a-zA-Z0-9.]+")
```

### Replacement and Substitution

#### **a. str_replace(string,pattern,repl)** :

Replaces the first match of a string pattern

```{r}
# let's find the digits part and replace it with a text
birthday <- "Your birthday is on January 7,1995"
str_replace(birthday,"\\d{4}",'Nineteen ninety-five')
```

#### **b. str_replace_all(string, pattern, repl)**

Replaces all matches of the pattern

```{r}
contract <- "Your two phone numbers are 0245768526 and 0241369095"
str_replace_all(contract,'\\d{10}','XXXXXXX')
```

### Splitting & Combining

This part of string function is for splitting and combine strings using string r**:**

#### **a. str_split(string,pattern)**

This splits a string passed on the pattern you supply and it splits into a list:

```{r}
# Example : say i want to split my string based on the separator (-)
case <- "Samuel-1993-CompScience"
str_split(case,"-")
```

```{r}
# Let's take a second example :
data <- c("HIV,Positive,2024", "TB,Negative,2023")
str_split(data, ",")
```

```{r}
# Let's take another more example: splitting by multiple delimeters
text <- c("Glucose=120;BMI=30", "Glucose=140;BMI=28")
str_split(text, "[=;]")
```

#### b. str_split_fixed(string, pattern, n)

Say you want to return a structured results after splitting information, then str_split_fixed() is what you need. it allows you to add how many columns you want the captured patterns to be spread into

```{r}
# let's take this example :
data <- c("HIV,Positive,2024", "TB,Negative,2023")
str_split_fixed(data, ",", 3)
```

#### Combining strings :

#### a. str_c(x,y, sep = "")

The cleanest way to concatenate(join) strings in R

```{r}
# say we want to combine these two strings
str_c('hello','world',sep = " ")
```

```{r}
# say we want to combine first and second names from two vectors
first_name <- c("Samuel", "Ama", "Kojo")
last_name  <- c("Abugare","Mensah", "Owusu")
full_name <- str_c(first_name,last_name, sep = " ")
full_name
```

Note that for the functions above, similar function exist in base R: Example for str_c() in stringr, base R has paste() which basically does the same thing. In my opinion, stringr function names are more descriptive than base R :

```{r}
# let's do the above with paste in Base R
paste(first_name,last_name, sep = " ")
```

#### b. str_flatten(vector, collapse = "")

Collapses a vector into one string

```{r}
# let's look at the name vectors : first name
str_flatten(first_name,collapse = " ")
```

### Case Conversion

Case conversion comprises of many function for converting string to a specific case:

#### a. str_to_upper(), str_to_lower(), str_to_title() etc

```{r}
# let's work on some examples 
text <- 'Today is our day'
# upper case
str_to_upper(text)
# lower case 
str_to_lower(text)
# title case
str_to_title(text)
# string to sentence case
str_to_sentence(text)
```

### Padding, Trimming & Formatting

Control whitespace and width

```{r}
# let's take some example 
my_string <- "  you can't have her  "

# trim left
str_trim(my_string, side = 'left')
# trim right
str_trim(my_string, side = "right")

# trim both sides
str_trim(my_string, side = "both")

```

Trimming is very important to be done on data before matching , joining or comparisons are mad**e**

```{r}
# cleaning messy data : 
names <- c(" John", "Mary ", "  Alice  ")
str_trim(names)
```

```{r}
# str_trim cannot remove whitespaces between text 
bn_ws <- c(" John  Slick", "Nathaniel    Hyde")
# this removes the extra white spaces between the names
str_squish(bn_ws)
```

#### `str_pad()`

This function is used to **make all strings the same length by adding extra characters (padding)**.

```{r}
# Let's take an example :
fruits <- c('guava','weed','cucumber')
str_pad(fruits, width = 7, side = "both", pad = " ")
```

### Length & Position

Measure or locate things in a string

```{r}
# length of string: gives the length of the string: if vector, length of each item
str_length(fruits)
# same as base r nchar()
nchar(fruits)
```

#### a. str_locate()

finds the start and end position of a pattern in a string : counting of characters includes spaces. finds only first match

```{r}
x <- "You are on12 and can't have nothing"
str_locate(x, pattern = "\\d+")
```

#### b. str_locate_all()

locate the start and end position of all matches of the pattern in the string

```{r}
x1 <- "old age has come 10 times but i have dodged 60 times"
str_locate_all(x1,"\\d+")
```

### Interpolation & Templating

Used to embed variables in strings:

**a. str_glue(str, variable)**

```{r}
# Let's call this email in our string

email <-'samuelabugare@gmail.com'
str_glue("my email is: {email}")

# you can use paste from base R to get the same effect
paste('My email is :', email)
```

**b. str_glue_data(str, variable)**

It’s used to create strings by inserting variables **directly from a data frame (or list/environment)** into a template.

```{r}
df <-  data_frame(
  name = c("samuel",'Johnny','Emma','Manuel'),
  age = c(22,32,12,45)
)
str_glue_data(df, "Name : {name}, Age : {age}")
```

```{r}
# let's take another example 
bio_info <- tibble(
  name = c('Jane','Molly','Dareen'),
  glucose = c(5.1,4.9,3.3)
)
# let's do something interesting 
str_glue_data(
  bio_info,
  "Patient : {name} your blood glucose is {ifelse(glucose >3.5,'High','Normal')}"
)
```

```{r}
# more examples
df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:3,
  date = Sys.Date()
)
# let's create files by id and date
str_glue_data(df, "report_{id}_{date}.csv")
```

### Forcats — Taming Categorical Variables

Factors are R's representation of categorical variables. forcats provides tools for reordering, relabeling, and collapsing factor levels operations that have an outsized impact on the quality of visualizations and models.why factor matters: without factor, R treat categories as plain strings

### **Creating factors :**

#### a. factor(), b. as_factor(), c. as.factor() : as_factor is tidyverse forcats the rest are base R

```{r}
# when you load tidyverse it is part of it but you can load it separately
library(forcats)
# you can convert to factor by using any of these: but factor allows you to reorder
status <- c("low", "high", "medium", "low", "high")
stats_f <- factor(status,levels = c("low","medium","high"))
stats_g <- as_factor(status)
class(status)
class(stats_f)
class(stats_g)
```

#### b. Checking number of levels, level counts etc

```{r}
# show levels 
levels(stats_f)

# shows total count of unique levels
nlevels(stats_f)
```

```{r}
# counts number of observations under each level
fct_count(stats_f)
```

```{r}
# shows unique factors in the series or vector
fct_unique(stats_f)
```

### Reordering Levels

The most common use case — controls how bars/lines appear in ggplot2

```{r}
f <- factor(c("banana", "apple", "cherry", "apple", "banana", "banana"))
fct_count(f)
```

#### a. order by frequency and first appearance

```{r}
# default levels
levels(f)
cat("----------------------------------------\n")
# Order by frequency (most common first) : see the levels below changed
fct_infreq(f)
```

```{r}
# order by first appearance : reorders by how they appear in the original data
fct_inorder(f)
```

#### b. Reversing current order

```{r}
# reverses the current order : see the order reveresed 
fct_rev(f)
```

```{r}
# manually changing order like in factor(vector, levels = (x,y,z))
fct_relevel(f,"banana",'apple','cherry')
```

```{r}
# Relevel by moving one level to front: see cherry comes first
fct_relevel(f, "cherry")
```

### Let's work on more examples with a data frame:

We can reorder a factor by another variable: instead of ordering by say frequency or as in they originally occur or appear, we can order by another variable. say we want to reorder department by salary

```{r}
# creating a data frame
survey <- data.frame(
  dept   = c("HR", "IT", "Finance", "IT", "HR", "HR"),
  salary = c(50, 90, 75, 95, 52, 48)
)
head(survey,4)
```

```{r}
# let's reorder the dept by salary: reorder the dept by mean salary in descending order 

survey1 <- survey |> 
  mutate(
    dept = fct_reorder(dept,salary, .fun = mean, .desc = TRUE)
  )
levels(survey1$dept)
```

Let's plot this :

```{r fig.dpi=300, fig.height= 7, fig.width= 14}
ggplot(
  survey, aes(x = fct_reorder(dept,salary,.fun = mean,.desc = TRUE), y = after_stat(count))
)+
  geom_col(
    stat = 'count',
    fill = "coral2",
    width = 0.5
  )+
  labs(
    title = "Factor reordering example",
    x = "Department",
    y = "Salar($)",
    caption = "Source: sambuganalytics"
  )+
  geom_text(
    stat = "count",
    aes(label = paste(after_stat(count),"people"),
        vjust = -0.4)
  )+
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 3,
    color = "lightpink",
    linewidth = 1.2,
    linetype = "dashed"
  )+annotate(
  "text",
  x = 2,
  y = 3,
  label = "Threshold = 3",
  hjust = 1.1,   # pushes slightly inside from the right edge
  vjust = -0.5,
  color = "black",
  size = 4
)+
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size =11),
    axis.text =  element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    plot.caption = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

### Renaming Levels

Functions to be considered here are for recoding or renaming factors : Sometimes you have factors in format or levels you don't want and would want to recode, fct-recode() does the work:

#### a.fct_recode(vector, "new_name"= "old name1), 'new_name2"= "oldname2")

```{r}
# let's look at how to do that with this vector
f <- factor(c("M", "F", "F", "M", "M"))

# factor recode
fct_recode(f, 
           "Female"= "F",
           "Male"= "M")
```

#### b. fct_relabel(vector, function)

```{r}
# let's look at this example 
gender <- factor(c("male",'female','male','male','female'))

# let's make them title case
fct_relabel(gender, str_to_title)
```

```{r}
# let's add put in another function for the relabelling: 
# Let's add sex_ to each level in gender
fct_relabel(gender, \(x) paste0("sex_",x))
```

### **Collapsing and lumping levels**

Reduce many categories into fewer ones; for instance you have male, female and wants to lump the remaining gender identity into something like others.

#### **a. fct_lump_n(vector, n)**

Keeps top n most frequent levels and returns the rest as others

```{r}
# Let's take this example 
brand <- factor(c("Nike","Adidas","Puma","Reebok","Fila","Nike","Adidas","Nike"))

# let's lump the first two most frequent brands and then the rest
fct_lump_n(brand, n = 2) 
```

it reorders the brand into Adidas, Nike and Other. Adidas and Mike are the top two most frequent brands and then the rest lump into others.

#### b. fct_lump_min(vector, min = x)

keep factors that appear at least min times and then lumps the rest into other

```{r}
# Keep levels that appear at least min times
fct_lump_min(brand, min = 2)
```

#### c. fct_lump_prop(vector, prop = 0.x)

keep factors above a certain proportion and then lump the rest as other

```{r}
# Keep levels that appear at least min times
fct_lump_prop(brand, prop = 0.3)
```

#### d. Collapse levels into groups

sometimes you might want to put more levels under one big level

```{r}
# let's take an example :
fct_collapse(brand,
  "Big3"  = c("Nike", "Adidas", "Puma"),
  "Other" = c("Reebok", "Fila")
)
```

### Adding & Dropping Levels

We are looking at how to add or remove levels from a factor vector:

#### a. fct_drop(vector, level)

```{r}
# Drop levels that have no observations
f2 <- factor(c("cat", "dog"), levels = c("cat", "dog", "bird"))
fct_drop(f2)          # removes "bird"
```

We can remove specific level by specifying the specific unused level.

```{r}
fct_drop(f2, "bird")  # drop a specific unused level
```

```{r}
# we can drop levels after filtering by a specific factor level
survey |> 
  filter(dept == "IT") |> 
  mutate(dept = fct_drop(dept))   # removes HR, Finance from levels
```

**You have to explicitly drop levels after filtering by a factor level:**

```{r}
# lets' demonstrate the levels we have after filtering
dept_reg <- survey |> 
  mutate(dept = factor(dept)) |> 
  filter(dept == "IT")
levels(dept_reg$dept)
```

### Handling NA & Unknown Values

#### a. fct_na_value_to_level(vector, level = "level_name")

```{r}
# let's demonstrate with some examples:
f <- factor(c("yes", "no", NA, "yes", NA))

# making NA a specific level:
fct_na_value_to_level(f, level = "Unknown")
```

### Changing Level Order by Shuffling

sometimes you might want to shuffle the levels for all possible reasons.

```{r}
f <- factor(c("a", "b", "c", "d"))
# let's see the original order 
levels(f)
cat("----------------------------------------------")
# Randomly shuffle levels (useful for simulations)
fct_shuffle(f)
```

**shift levels left or right by n position**

```{r}
# Shift levels left or right by n positions
levels(f)
fct_shift(f, n = 1)   # shifts left; moves each element one step backward
fct_shift(f, n = -1)  # shifts right : moves each element one step forward
```

### Real-World Workflow Example

```{r}
# Simulate a customer satisfaction dataset
set.seed(42)
df <- data.frame(
  region  = sample(c("North", "South", "East", "West", "Central"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  rating  = sample(c("Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  score   = runif(200, 1, 10)
)

df |> 
  mutate(
    # Fix natural order of ordinal variable
    rating = fct_relevel(rating, "Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent"),

    # Lump small regions into "Other"
    region = fct_lump_n(region, n = 3),

    # Rename a level
    region = fct_recode(region, "Midwest" = "Central")
  ) |> 
  group_by(region, rating) |> 
  summarise(avg_score = mean(score), .groups = "drop") %>%

  # Plot with correct ordering
  ggplot(aes(x = rating, y = avg_score, fill = region)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Avg Score by Rating and Region")
```
